column6: Tools for Mathematics and the Sciences: Algebra
column19: This course will expose students to certain basic tools and calculations in algebra. Some of the material may be familiar to those who studied mathematics in high school. Familiarity with the material discussed in this course may be assumed in subsequent courses across various disciplines including mathematics and physics. In an article titled ‘The unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in the natural sciences’, physicist Eugene Wigner wrote “… the enormous usefulness of mathematics in the natural sciences is something bordering on the mysterious and that there is no rational explanation for it”. Mathematics has emerged as the natural language using which the laws governing the working of the universe can be described; it is also a discipline with a rich internal structure explored through powerful frameworks for description and justification. Whether one is studying black holes or neural networks, molecular bonds or climate models, tiling patterns or cryptography, the use of mathematics is unavoidable. A solid foundation of mathematics is therefore an essential part of the skill set required of every student of the natural sciences; a good grasp of basic tools, examples, and calculations is also essential for those planning to study mathematics in greater depth and rigour. Note: This course does not count as a required or elective course contributing to the graduation requirements in either Mathematics or Physics.

This course aids students in donning multiple hats so as to understand the respective decision-making process of different fiduciary stakeholders that are based on financial statements of a reporting entity. For example, shareholders use accounting information to determine the intrinsic value of the stock, which helps them to decide whether to buy, hold, or sell the company’s share. Bankers and lenders rely on firm’s financial statements in order to decide whether to lend money or not to firms. The course also discusses the significance of relevant accounting standards and the evolving regulatory landscape in the preparation and interpretation of financial statements. This course is also designed to provide students with a deeper understanding of nature and workings of corporate financial management. The course aims to provide the framework, concepts, and tools for analysing financial decisions based on fundamental principles of modern financial theory. It introduces the students to the many ways in which corporate management both evaluates investment opportunities and finances investments. It also teaches basic financial concepts and provides students with the tools necessary for evaluating the intrinsic value of a corporation, as well as assessing a corporation's effectiveness in maximizing its value. Further, the course highlights the important real-world applications of the various theories.

Introduction: 
Accounting is the language of Business: Manufacturing and trading entities are important organs of the world’s economic dimension. The economic dimension of the world is often described as economy.
 In an economy, financial transactions are inherent.  Companies and other entities need to communicate to the employees and the public and statutory administrative bodies about the transactions they perform which have financial implications.  This need is precisely addressed by a language called accounting. Accounting framework is an important edifice like technical, legal and other entities.
Accounting is perhaps the single largest edifice of a business edifice with, and around, which the whole gamut of other edifices are built and intertwined. 
Accounting is very often the basis for decision making – both internal and external. Whether to increase prices or cut costs or “Buy, Sell or Hold” decisions, companies need to have their accounting systems in place. 
Course Design:
The Course on Advanced Topics in Accounting is designed with the following focus: 
1.        To enable students to understand certain advanced Accounting standards 
2.        To enable students to better appreciate the contents of financial statements – to be read along with other aspects of annual reports (like Chairman’s report / Board of Directors report) 
3.        To enable students to apply various management accounting tools used for decision making and control especially in the context of Strategic Cost Management

The course deals with Principles and Practices of People Management in organizations as relevant to the roles and responsibilities of managers across functions. It develops a detailed understanding of the people management process- Workforce planning, Recruitment and Selection, Training and Development, Performance Management System, Labor Laws and Employee relations etc.

Course Coverage:
Financial Management
Time value of money – advanced concepts
Investment Appraisal Techniques
Technical and Fundamental Analysis
Risk Management – Options, Futures, Forwards and Risk Management
Learning Outcomes:
At the end of the course, the students would be able to:
1. Understand general and specific cash flows, based on which financial analysis is carried out
2. Apply investment appraisal techniques to determine the financial feasibility of the projects
3. Valuation of shares and bonds; determination of WACC
4. Use of fundamental & technical analysis to determine the value of a share / company / business.
5. Determine working capital requirements of a business and how to optimize the same
6. Advanced topics in Financial Management – including options & futures (to manage risk better)

column6: Introduction to Financial Time Series Forecasting
column18: ECON204 OR ECON212|DATA212 OR MATH314 OR PSYC211
column19:
Forecasting is an emerging domain in the field of business during this time. In Finance
and Economics, we need to know about the value of risk, volatility, asset pricing,
portfolio allocations, interest rate modelling, and inflation rate. The forecasting
technique helps them to get an idea about the risk factors. This course aims to provide a
strong foundation of forecasting and time series econometrics and financial risk

undergraduates. This course bridges the gap between academia and the corporate world by
equipping students with the mental models, skills, behaviours, and business awareness needed
to transition confidently into the workplace.
Students learn how organizations function, how companies create value, how to navigate
workplace culture and expectations, and how to build a strong professional identity.
The course is structured to level the playing field for new entrants to the corporate world -
focused on empowerment, awareness, and competitive advantage.

The Principles of Economics course introduces students to foundational economic principles, introducing tools and models that enable a rigorous examination of everyday economic phenomena. It presents fundamental theories in micro- as well as macroeconomics, covering markets and prices, trade-offs, efficiencies, externalities, as well as the behavior of individuals and firms. The course initiates an examination of broader systemic phenomena such as trade, growth, poverty, employment, and inequality. At the end of the course, students should be familiar with foundational economic terminology, develop a basic understanding of markets and their potential failures, begin to appreciate the linkages between economic phenomena, and most importantly, recognize the importance of a rigorous approach in exploring economic questions.
column21: Preference given to students in year 1.

column19: This course is a sequel to Microeconomics I, and will focus on the study of producer behavior. We begin with a stylized model of the firm, and then understand how economists model production, and how firms minimize their costs and maximize their profits. With a basic understanding of consumer and producer behavior, we will then look at how the two interact in a market. The concept of the market equilibrium will be introduced, and we will learn how the characteristics of this equilibrium vary across different market structures such as perfectly competitive markets, monopoly and oligopoly. We will then learn about conditions where the market fails to achieve an equilibrium, focusing on externalities, public goods, and markets with asymmetric information.
column21: Preference given to students in year 2; also open to year 3/4 students graduating in 2026 for whom this is a required course.

column19: This course is a sequel to Macroeconomics I. It builds on the basic models introduced in Macroeconomics I, and introduces theories of unemployment and inflation, the inflation-output trade off, natural rate of unemployment, and the Phillips curve. It then shifts focus to the long run and introduces students to the economics of growth, the role of capital accumulation and technological progress, as well as policy related aspects of economic growth.
column21: Preference given to students in year 2; also open to year 3/4 students graduating in 2026 for whom this is a required course.

column19:
The economy, which we have come to think of as a distinct sphere of human activity, is a peculiar conceptual construct with an even more peculiar history. This course introduces economics majors to influential intellectual traditions that continue to shape how we think about the economy and the laws that govern it. Along the way, the class will revisit and historicize commonplace categories in the field of economics: commodity, money, capital, prices, wages and rents, supply and demand, business cycles, and so on. 
 
 The course begins with the 18th century, when the field of political economy was still in its nascent stage. The first three weeks of the course focus on the classical tradition of political economy, centred around the work of Adam Smith and David Ricardo. This is followed by two weeks of Marxian political economy, and two weeks on neo-classical economic thought. After an excursus into institutional, socialist, utopian, and historical traditions in economics, the course concludes with a deep engagement with the Keynesian revolution and its lasting influence on the field. Students will also read and engage with work that looks at how intellectual currents in political economy and economics shaped modern institutions, in European nations, in India, and in global governance.
column21: Preference given to students graduating in 2026 for whom this is a required course.

column19: This course will examine the links between economic and ecological systems. We will use concepts from welfare economics, common pool resources, ecosystem valuation and environmental ethics and apply them to the problems of fisheries and forest management, biodiversity conservation and global environmental change. The course will also focus on the relationship between economic growth, ecosystem services and human flourishing in pursuit of sustainable development.
column21: Capped at 30;  Preference given to year 3/4 students graduating in 2026.

column19:
This course introduces students to key topics in the field of Development economics and policy, particularly those centered around the colossal challenges facing the global poor.
The first part of the course will introduce students to the fundamental question of why we still see extreme levels of poverty around the world, why some countries are rich while the others are poor. We will review selected classical and contemporary models of development to explore structural and institutional factors that impact the process of development. The second part of the course will dive deep into the concept of poverty at a micro level, i.e., at the level of individuals and households. The course will introduce and encourage students to think about how the poor make decisions, what constraints they face and what difficult trade-offs they make. We will learn about the actions and policies taken by various entities (Governments, international organizations, and NGOs) to improve the lives of the poor. Using modern empirical techniques, we will understand which of these policies have been successful, and which have not. 
At the end of the course, the students will develop a deeper appreciation for the dynamics of the development process and the challenges involved in ending poverty across the world, and have a better understanding of how poverty affects various aspects of human development.

There is today a definite mainstream in macroeconomics. While ideas that do not fit into this received framework tend to be ignored they can be crucial to understanding the working of the world economy, including India’s. Some of these are part of an entire approach to macroeconomics while others are standalone ideas/constructs addressing issues as broad as economic growth and as specific as financial crises. This course aims to introduce students with these heterodox approaches and ideas, with a view to enhancing their understanding of both how economic issues have been framed and how the economy actually works. The course is meant for students with an interest in economic ideas and evidence-based analysis of the economy.

The course will review a variety of evaluation designs for assessing the impact of interventions, may it be policies, programs or products, in the context of implementation research. The concept of counterfactual and causality will be discussed. The importance of considering mixed methods approach to impact evaluation will be highlighted. Mixed methods approach combines quantitative methods, qualitative methods as well as process evaluation for monitoring of the intervention. Practical examples from LEAD’s own work as well as from other published studies in the social sector will be used throughout the duration of the course.

column19: This course delves into the economic aspects of education, with a specific focus on developing nations. It begins by tracing the historical trajectory of the economics of education, positioning it as a pivotal discipline amidst a broad spectrum dedicated to educational studies. Through an economic lens, it thoroughly examines diverse research avenues within education, such as human capital theory, educational production, cost analysis, funding mechanisms, educational planning, teacher dynamics, and the dynamics of educational markets and choice. The exploration involves not only the scrutiny of economic theories but also practical implications encompassing educational policies.

column6: Introduction to Finance: Concepts and Methods
column19:
The Great Recession of 2008 dealt an important lesson to economists – that the real economy and the financial world are closely interconnected and lacking an understanding the world of finance is no longer tenable for economists. An understanding of finance and how the world of finance operates is an essential ingredient in the toolkit for a practicing economist. With this motivation, this First Course in Finance is designed to provide an introduction to the world of finance. As a first course, it gives an introductory glimpse into the various parts of the field of finance. For anyone planning to gain deeper understanding in the field of finance by taking additional more intense courses in finance, this course serves as a preparatory, foundational step. By providing a comprehensive overview of the subject it would also serve students who are seeking only a basic but broad understanding of finance.
This course is focused on business finance, to the exclusion of personal finance and public finance. Starting with a definition of finance as the organizing principle, the course content is structured around agents that demand finance for business, namely, business organisations. The first part of the course develops an understanding of the business organization – its goals, its forms, and the accounting of its financial transactions. The financial accounts are key to keep track of the financial health of the business. A healthy business generates finance internally and is also able to access external sources relatively easily for its daily business needs and also for investments. The second part of the course covers concepts and methods relating to business investments, like valuing cash flows from investments, and profitability and risk in investments. Business finance is accessed in financial markets through financial institutions that intermediate between savers and the borrowing business organisations. The third part of the course covers these aspects – sources of finance, financial markets and financial institutions. Finally, we look at how prices are determined in the financial markets – bond prices, stock prices, exchange rates – and how this links to the macroeconomy. We also take a brief overview of quantitative finance, which provides a toolkit for financial analysts and managers.

column19: The present course uses gender as a lens for looking into the history of medieval and early-modern South Asia. It especially looks at the categories of ‘masculinity’ and ‘ femininity’, how these were constructed and mapped during the period, in relation to one another. In doing so, it considers how evolving ideals of manliness came to inform kingship and domesticity in the Sultanate and the Mughal period. To what extent was the courtly and domestic spaces segregated? What were the ways in which the royal women responded and negotiated with the prescribed norms and participate in politics and court society ? How had art and architectural productions served as sites of gendered patronage, aesthetics, labour and performance ? These are some of the questions that we will address in this course. The course will also explore the non-royal social and political groups, the concubines, dancing girls, women slaves and labourers as well as the gender-liminal figure of the eunuch. The processes of gender marginalisation and defiance of gender normativity will also be taken up, particularly through a study of some of the women saints who challenged societal hierarchies in their pursuit of spirituality. The course will culminate with a discussion on how the notions of gender normativity were reoriented and subverted at the wake of colonialism in the eighteenth century.

column6: Diversity and Unity in Medieval Europe 500-1500 CE
column19: Too often, especially in Europe itself, the European trajectory of history is taken to be not just a typical template, but one which somehow explains how this relatively small portion of the globe found a path to world domination. We miss too easily that that domination was really achieved by only three or four of Europe’s very numerous polities, not even all the largest ones, and that the continent remained and remains broken up and contentious in identity, even though it is often treated and even acts like a single politico-religious entity. This course looks at Europe’s first and formative millennium, and tries to distinguish what worked against its unity and maintained its distinct identities and practices, as well as the more usual opposite. Looking especially at religion and government, as well as the basic resources of life, it sets out to make clearer how Europe’s foundations mean it has never quite been one thing together, despite how much its components share.

column6: West Asia and the Mediterranean 200-700 CE: Empires, Religions and Replacement
column19: The early centuries of the Common Era in West Asia are dominated in historiography by two opposed empires, that of the Romans and that of the Persians. Arguably the whole of European history, which has subsequently been exported to much of the globe, is the process of dealing with and occasionally trying to reverse the end of the Roman culture; Persia, though less well-recorded, is no less significant for its inheritors, Islamic and otherwise. This course charts the entwined fates of the two empires in their long final phase, which ended with their replacement, in whole or in part, by a new competitor in the form of the first Islamic caliphate. Religion, ethnic identity and ideas about power come to the fore in this course, which will leave you understanding better both the shape of the world which West Asia has affected today and the enduring cultural significance of Rome, and Persia, as archetypes and aspirations.

How do we make sense of India? Is India a rich country with poor people? Is it a scientific superpower or a land of superstition? Answering these questions requires an understanding of the contemporary history of India. We will first look through the first fifty-three years of Indian independence to see how different political parties rose and fell, how society and the environment have shaped politics, how India’s foreign policy is made and how the leadership styles of different Indian Prime Ministers varied. We will study a wide variety of important personalities including Jawaharlal Nehru, the Dalai Lama, Lalu Prasad Yadav, Salman Khan and Amartya Sen. We will also look at interesting changes in Indian history from the writing of the constitution to the 1962 Sino-Indian war to the rise of McDonalds. The course will be of interest to students of Indian history, politics and society. More broadly it will be of interest to anyone who is interested in the historical events that defined the lives of their parents and grandparents.

column19:
History is not simply the study of what happened in the past. It also involves reflections on the nature of the past itself and how we come to know it. Such reflections on the ontology of the past, our ability to access it and the narrative forms in which the past is presented – have all been extensively discussed in the philosophy of history and historiography. Combining theories and insights from metaphysics, epistemology, hermeneutics and ethics, this course intends to explore the nature of historical thinking and reasoning. As such, this course has two objectives. First, to seek conceptual understanding of categories such as past, time, history, myth, chronology, causation, historical necessity and contingency. Second, this course also explores some key
 questions often raised in the philosophy of history: How do we know, represent and explain the past? Is historical truth objective and absolute or relative and contingent? Does history have meaning or direction? What do historical accounts focus on – individual actions, social structures, cultures, nations and civilizations, different time periods? Finally, do historical accounts carry moral imperatives? To respond to these questions, we will study a number of thinkers such as Vico, Herder, Hegel, Marx, Nietzsche, Collingwood, Michel Foucault, Paul Ricoeur, Hayden White and Ankersmit. Course readings will include a combination of selections from the writings of above-mentioned thinkers and accessible scholarly writings.

This course introduces ancient civilizations, specifically focusing on the Indus Valley with discussions on Mesopotamia, Egypt, and China, and an overview of developments in other regions of Asia, Africa, and the Americas. We discuss alternate theories regarding urbanisation and definitions of civilizations. We also highlight discoveries and theoretical and methodological approaches in archaeology that have influenced interpretations of diverse civilizations. The course highlights transformations from early agro-pastoral Neolithic cultures with an emphasis on examining cultural transitions, the origins of agriculture, and the spread of domesticated plants and animals. We discuss the influence of environmental changes on the rise, spread, and decline of civilizations. We highlight issues related to the diverse manifestations of settlements, urban architecture and spatial organisation, governance, socio-economic structures, intellectual and religious lives, technologies, architecture, literature, art/craft, and more. The course discusses ancient population migrations as inferred from archaeological, linguistic, and genetic studies. It concludes by situating ancient worlds within modern contexts as related to changing perceptions and constructions of the past.

How do you stage a revolution? Why do revolutions happen at some places and times but not others? What will the revolutions of the future look like? These are some the questions that this course will try to answer. Starting with the cognitive revolution thousands of years ago and ending with the ongoing revolution in artificial intelligence, this course will tell the story of world history through social as well as political revolutions. We will look not only at the four great political revolutions in America, Russia, France and China but also at many smaller ones that shape our world in subtle ways from Haiti to Vietnam. We will also study several social revolutions that have been no less instrumental in shaping humanity from the industrial revolution to the sexual revolution. We will explore the causes, ideologies and methods that animated revolutionaries as well as the impact of many of these revolutions on life in the present. In doing so we will also learn about key themes in historiography such as change, contingency, agency and progress.

column6: The Art and Architecture of Medieval South Asia
column19:
Is it possible to read physical objects such as paintings and works of architecture as manifestations of economic, political, social and environmental transformation in Medieval South Asia? Given the extent to which scholars have come to rely on texts to narrate the history of medieval South Asia, when and for what reasons might one turn towards physical artifacts and objects as sources of historical information? This course answers the aforementioned questions by bringing attention to artifactual cultures spanning 550 years in South Asia, beginning towards the end of the 12th century and concluding in the mid- eighteenth century. 
 
 The course commences with framing questions around “the medieval” in South Asian History and the ways in which that concept comes to inform debates around community and stateformation, the exercise of sovereignty and power, religiosity, patronage, travel, colonialism, and more recently, populism and nationalism. Subsequently, the course explores the ways in which the periodization of the medieval comes to encompass visual artifacts spanning the Ghurid, Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Vijayanagara, Sharqi, Lodhi and Mughal periods. The course ends with the debates surrounding the emergence of an “early modern period” in South Asian history and the peculiar manner in which the artefactual culture of medieval south Asia comes into conversation with that of the early modern. At the broadest level the course will not only introduce students to a wide array of works of art and architecture in the region, it will also encourage them to develop interpretative descriptions of these works by drawing on a variety of primary and secondary sources.

column6: Self, State and Society: Philosophical Perspectives
column19: There is an intricate dialectical relation between the concepts of self, state and society, and these relations are negotiated in every age, differently. It is important to understand these relations, as they provide us with the rationale for our understanding of ourselves, and our place in the social and political domains. These relations also determine the possibilities and limits of our own agency and actions vis-à-vis others. This course will introduce some of the fundamental philosophical presuppositions that allow this negotiation to take place in the modern age. The course is divided into three modules that discuss the constitution of the self, the state, and the social, in the contemporary modern western age. The objective of this discussion is to not only present a philosophical analysis of these concepts but to also open them up for critique and alternative readings, either from the classical tradition or in some cases contemporary perspectives. The course is not intended to be comprehensive in its approach to the readings presented, but rather the focus is to have an in-depth engagement with the philosophical presuppositions of the perspectives presented. Some of the fundamental issues taken up would be: How is the notion of the self, constituted and what relation does it bear to the understanding of the modern age, and the state? What are the fundamental presuppositions that characterise the foundations of the modern state? What are some of the theoretical alternatives to this understanding of the state? What is the role of the social, as presented through the institution of the family, in this matrix? What is the relation that the family bears to the state, and the self?

How do we reason about reason? Are there underlying principles that can connect reasoning about philosophical abstractions, legal and politics argument, analysis of texts, scientific and social scientific theorisations, solving puzzles and writing mathematical proofs? Can we make precise what we mean by reason or codify what we mean by a reasonable argument? How have philosophers lent meaning to make sense of the human quest to discover the laws of reason?

This course attempts to trace the long standing intellectual project of identifying the laws of deductive reasoning. We begin with historical attempts and philosophical underpinnings underlying these attempts, before diving deep into contemporary formal frameworks that fall under the aegis of logic.

In the process, we use precise formulations of deductive reasoning using symbolic abstractions which enables us to answer the following questions:

How do we ensure that a set of sentences are mutually consistent?
How do we make sense of paradoxes?
How do we ensure that deductive arguments are logically sound?
What can and cannot be deduced from a given collection of statements?
How do we reason precisely when confronted with ambiguities such as knowledge or lack of it, and belief and contingency?

We further extend our set of questions to attempt to answer the following questions about the method of reasoning itself:

What kind of statements are amenable to formal deductive reasoning?
What is the nature of the relationship between reasoning and language?
How do we reason within a given formal reasoning system as well as about a given formal reasoning system?

The course intends to provide access to ideas and contemporary vocabulary which will enable to deploy logic as a means to reason within philosophy, as well as enable pursuit logic and philosophy of logic as philosophical disciplines. Further it will bring alive challenges which makes the process of sound reasoning difficult even for sophisticated Artificial Intelligence tools today.

column6: Reading Aesthetics, Writing Modernity: Sanskrit Poetics and Indian Literature
column19: This course is for literature and philosophy students and bridges classical Indian aesthetic theory (Sanskrit and philosophy) with modern literary and comparative theory (vernacular, global, and historical frameworks) to trace the continuities, transformations, and re-framings of Indian aesthetic concepts across time and languages. The first half of the course traces the historical development of aesthetic and literary theorization in the Indian context. The discussion relies on two of the major schools of Sanskrit poetics– the Rasa school of Bharata and the Dhvani school of Ānandavardhana. It will shed light on how Indian aesthetic thought shifted from performance to language and from expression to interpretation. This section concludes with discussing how modern Indian philosophers revisited classical theories and reinterpreted them for the modern reader. In the second half of the course, the goal is to explore how modern Indian literary thinkers connected literary history, vernacular modernity, and the classical past. We will discuss moments of nationalist transformation and recasting of the Sanskritic tradition, questions of comparativism between languages, and the emergence of counter-cultural stances that query the hegemony of a singular tradition. How did writers, critics, and philosophers create bridges between the śāstraic and the modern, between kāvya and sāhitya?

column6: Global Politics I (Formerly known as POLT205 - Global Politics in the 21st Century (An Introduction))
column19: This course offers a general introduction to global politics by combining historical insights, conceptual tools and empirical accounts connected to international issues. The course begins with a brief historical review of political formations and conceptual overview of international relations. Contemporary issues of identity, inclusion, justice and welfare are examined in subsequent weeks, complicating traditional academic perspectives by considering real world debates and cases. Writing exercises, individual and group research projects and informed, structured discussions will be supplemented by lectures as needed.

column6: Political Imaginings from the Global South
column19: This course will introduce a complex world of ideas connected to society and politics created by thinkers and political actors of the Global South. Although a majority of thinkers discussed in this course will be from postcolonial societies of Africa, Latin America, and Asia, the term ‘Global South’, here, is not used as a spatial category but rather as a transnational subjectivity, a structure of sensibility shaped by the historical forces of colonialism, capitalism and nationalism. Ideas of society, politics, justice, and freedom as articulated in speech and text, and practiced in political organising, social mobilisation, resistance and rebellion, and education, by Frantz Fanon, B.R. Ambedkar, Babytai Kamble, Paolo Freire, Stephen Biko, Ho Chi Minh, Angela Davis, Kwame Ture, Jose Carlos Mariategui, Edward Said, and others will be discussed in this course, as well as more contemporary thinkers and practices building on these genealogies, including Linda Tuhiwai-Smith, Achille Mbembe, Chinnaiah Jangam, and EZLN. The course will encourage the students to interpret their work not only by placing them in their historical contexts but also by seeing their significance for contemporary times.

column6: Introduction to Political Theory: Concepts and Conundrums
column19:
This course is based on the conviction that theoretical concepts are indispensable to fully
 comprehend political realities and the ways in which they change. How do concepts emerge and
 develop, and what are the elements constitutive of their connection to empirical realities?
 Although abstract, political concepts are often deployed for the purpose of supporting as well as
 contesting concrete social arrangements, ideological positions, and institutions. They also act as
 necessary scaffold for alternative imaginings of political futures. This course is reading-intensive,
 and will pay close attention to the architecture of concepts as well as to their complex, and
 often conflicting, social mobilization. It is a course that highlights the connection between
 theory and practice, and explores new ways of doing political theory in our troubled and
 agonistic times.

column17: Dyotana Banerjee, Sudeshna Dey, Rekha Diwakar
column19: The purpose of this course is to introduce students to qualitative and quantitative modes of inquiry while understanding social and political phenomena. Through course material, students will become familiar with the philosophical foundations and perspectives of interpretive qualitative research and basic quantitative data. The course will highlight essential concepts and techniques, as well as explore key interpretive research questions such as the following: What kind of knowledge claims can be made and what counts as evidence to support those claims? How does a researcher’s positionality shape the direction, context, and the structures of power involved in the inquiry? What considerations regarding the representation of the ‘Other’ should a researcher address? What are the ethical issues that arise for interpretive researchers? In addition to such reflections during in-class discussions, students will also have an opportunity to develop their own qualitative and quantitative research proposal and conduct preliminary data collection. Through this preliminary process they will gain direct experience with the practice of research including developing an interpretive qualitative and quantitative research questions, crafting a research design, establishing a conceptual framework, engaging in data collection and analysis techniques, and learning some of the conventions of writing up research. By the end of the course, students will not only understand how qualitative and quantitative researchers produce knowledge but will also appreciate the possibilities of qualitative inquiry within quantitative research and vice versa.

column6: Caste in Critical Perspective: From Scriptural Order to Everyday Politics
column19:
This course offers a critical and interdisciplinary introduction to caste as a structure of power, a mode of social organization, and a lived experience in South Asia. Moving from scriptural origins to colonial codification, from ideological debates to embodied practices, the course unpacks how it continues to organise everyday life, maintain hierarchies, and shape access to dignity, justice and knowledge. Rather than treating caste as a static tradition, the course approaches it as a dynamic system sustained through everyday interaction and institutional design, yet constantly challenged by movements of resistance and assertion. Through a progression of thematic modules, students explore how caste is normalized and contested across time via scriptural codes and colonial enumeration as well as in ideological debates and sensory experiences.
The course begins by interrogating the religious and philosophical foundations of caste before examining how colonial governance transformed caste into a system of classification and political identity. It engages with the ideas of Ambedkar and Gandhi to highlight competing visions of reform and annihilation of caste. Moreover, students explore how caste operates through the body, gender, sexuality, memory and humiliation, and how it becomes tangible in practices of food, touch, smell and labour. The final module emphasizes academic responsibility by training students to write about caste critically with attention to standpoint and representation.
Drawing from sociology, politics, anthropology, Dalit studies, feminist theory, and cultural studies, the course uses a range of sources—including testimonies, autobiographies, ethnographies, films, and public texts. Emphasizing reflexive learning, it encourages students to connect theoretical debates to lived realities while developing intellectual rigor and sensitivity. The course fosters critical inquiry and social awareness, enabling students to question hierarchies and engage meaningfully with ongoing struggles for equality and dignity in anti-caste movements.

column6: Democracy and Autocracy in the Contemporary World
column19:
This course critically interrogates the notions of ‘democracy’ and ‘autocracy’ with empirical reference to the contemporary world of the early twenty-first century. So often juxtaposed as binary opposites along with related terms—freedom versus tyranny, liberty versus dictatorship—the line between democracy and authoritarianism has become empirically blurred a mere three decades after an American author proclaimed ‘the end of history’ with the ideological triumph of liberal democracy and its likely universalization. In the 1990s, the comparative study of ‘democratization’ was a booming sub-field of political science. In the 2020s, the scales have flipped and the comparative study of ‘autocratization’—also referred to as ‘democratic backsliding’—is a prime preoccupation of political scientists.
The abrupt swing of the pendulum shows that the binary distinction between ‘democracy’ and ‘authoritarianism’ in the 1990s and 2000s was an ideal-typical—and ideological—construct. The 2010s and 2020s represent a wake-up call to a far more complicated empirical reality, in which the politics of the leader of the Western/Euro- Atlantic ‘free world’ of democratic nations have taken an unexpected turn, along with that of the ‘world’s largest democracy’ in the non-Western world. The course is particularly focused on what the political scientists Stephan Haggard and Robert Kaufman call ‘the incremental erosion of institutions, rules, and norms that result from the actions of duly elected governments’ (and their leaders). This is a comparative politics course that draws on cases from around the world.
The Routledge Handbook of Autocratization (Aurel Croissant and Luca Tomini, eds), published in 2024, is a key course text. It consists of forty chapters organized in five parts. All the main readings for specific weeks are given below. The course will be offered in the third trimester of AY 2025-26.

column6: Nationalism and National Identity in the Contemporary World
column19:
Belying predictions and expectations around the beginning of the third millennium CE of the inexorable forward march of ‘globalization’ and the advent of a post-national age, passionate expressions of nationalist identity and pride animate and indeed dominate the politics of countries around the world. This is especially true of what Charles Tilly called ‘state-led nationalism’ and Benedict Anderson termed ‘official nationalism.’ Contemporary examples include the White, Christian brand of American nationalism championed by Donald Trump in the United States, the massive growth of English nationalism in Britain, the ascendancy of Hindu nationalism in India, and the rise to prominence and power of messianic forms of Zionism in Israel.
This course focuses on and explains the transition of these forms of nationalism from a deceptive marginality to the political centre-stage, and the transformation in their status from oppositional to mainstream and in some cases official ideologies of nation-statehood. The first part of the course covers the major theoretical perspectives on, approaches to the study of, and debates about nationalism and national identity. The second part is devoted to making sense of, and comparing, a selection of contemporary cases from different world regions. Nations and Nationalism: A Reader (Philip Spencer and Howard Wollman, eds, Edinburgh University Press, 2005) will be a key course text. The other major readings for each week are specified below. The course will be offered in the third trimester of AY 2025-26.

column6: South Asian Politics and International Relations
column19: The people of South Asia are bound by history and a common destiny, as they inhabit what Barry Buzan termed as a ‘security complex.’ That is, millennia of intersecting stories and a more recent shared colonial experience have brought them to their separate post-colonial journeys as modern states and societies. The course will review structures and issues of politics in each South Asian state (Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka), as well as conflict and cooperation between the states.

column6: Texts on Interrogating the Political and Social Imaginaries
column19: This seminar-based course explores critical political and social ideas regarding their constitution and deployment. Through the strategies of close and comparative readings, the course will highlight the entangled character of political visions and the struggles through which they occupy troubled residences in our part of the world.

This course focuses on infrastructural technologies as a mode of political power that operates on a planetary scale. Infrastructures are integral to the organisation of our collective life: the kinds of energy and material we use; the systems we build to extract and move material and energy around the planet; the ways in which we create and circulate value and waste; and the logics of property and space that shape and limit human (and nonhuman) mobility and accelerate the movement of capital. To understand these workings of power, we draw on recent theorisations of “planetary politics” that challenge us to go beyond our usual conceptions of political time and the placement of human agency at the centre of political life. 
 In our everyday lives, often seemingly mundane technical infrastructures shape our relationships to the nonhuman and to each other, inculcating norms of habit and sensing, and everyday rules and logistics, that come to have authority. At national and global scales, changes to our political economies of extractivism, production, information, and waste have restructured “politics as usual”, with consequences ranging from corporate capture in democratic politics to the shaping of new modes of authoritarianism. Our infrastructures entangle us in common logics that complicate many of our common distinctions of governance, public vs. private, centralisation and decentralisation, and political ideology. Drawing on multidisciplinary work in Science and Technology Studies, technopolitics, critical theory, and design, we will engage with a range of debates about how to grasp, theorise, and respond politically and collectively to forms of power enacted through our built structures and systems, their modes and logics of production, and the multiscalar, networked, and often diffused ways in which they work.

column6: Qualitative Methods: Researching the Social, Political and the Historical
column19: This course introduces the students to the various aspects, approaches and techniques of qualitative research. Qualitative research in social studies is significant for theory building and examining empiricism through exploration of the field. Distinct from quantitative methods, qualitative research methods involve close and long-standing interaction with the participants leading to various ethical and subjective considerations in research. This is also implicated in the researcher’s own location on and off the field. In addition, conducting field work involves multiple stages, sample selections, approaching and entering the field and planned process of observation. In the light of this, the course is divided into four sections. First section “Overview: key concepts and definitions” addresses the fundamental concepts related to qualitative research and the subject of methodological awareness required for conducting qualitative research. In the second module, “Various approaches of qualitative research”, the course offers detailed discussions on ethnography, case studies, life history method content and discourse analyses and the stages of theory building following an inductive approach to research. This module also extensively discusses the structural challenges and possibilities of conducting field work. The third module “Political economy of qualitative research” engages with the broad questions of how to conduct auto-ethnography and use the self as a research method; it deals with concepts like cultural insider, covert research etc. The fourth and the last module “Research Project” includes empirical research projects conducted by the students following various stages of qualitative research.

This course introduces key directions and themes in feminist thought and practice, both global and local, spanning a time frame starting from the eighteenth century to the contemporary times. Examining how gender and sexuality operates in society, we examine how gender is not an individual attribute or a role, but rather a system of social practices that constructs different categories of people—“men” and “women”—and organizes social interaction and inequality around this difference. The course will take a sociological approach in understanding what is sex and gender , how they operate in the labor market, at home, and at school, and how they structure our everyday lives at the individual, interactional, and institutional level. Throughout the course, we will prioritize reading, evaluating, and questioning feminist theory and sociological research on gender. We will also investigate feminist thought from a variety of disciplinary perspectives and theoretical orientations and focus on key debates such as the sex/gender system, intersectionality, sexual difference, and essentialism, amongst others. This course aims to think through the ways in which gender and sexuality intersect with caste, class, community and the nation. The aim of this course is to unravel the centrality of power in the practice of gender.

The human “propensity to truck, barter, and exchange” (a la Adam Smith) lies at the heart of all modern economies. And yet, social scientists have adopted widely diverging theoretical frameworks to understand how market economies function and evolve. At one end, the dominant strand of economics today takes rational and instrumental action by individuals as its starting point when modelling market exchange. By contrast, an equally influential stream of social thought assumes that economic behaviour is conditioned by the same set of social and political institutions that also govern other types of non-economic behaviour. In this course, students will be introduced to the latter set of intellectual traditions in political economy and economic sociology, wherein “institutions” are treated not merely as constraints upon economic behaviour but also as constitutive of both the preferences and norms that inform such behaviour.

The course is divided into two modules. The first module (four weeks) revisits the work of some original thinkers to locate the intellectual origins of this field of study. The second module poses a series of comparative and historical questions that help illustrate the evolution of the capitalist world economy from the 18th to the 21st century. Some of the possible themes to be covered in the second module will include: the great divergence, industrialization and financialization, inequality and social im/mobility, mass education and the establishment of professions, tax reforms and welfare states, and new social movements.

This course offers an accessible introduction to political anthropology by tracing how the field emerged, how it relates to allied disciplines, and what makes anthropological approach to power and politics distinctive. Through close readings of foundational texts, key theoretical debates, and ethnographic case studies from diverse contexts, students will explore how political anthropology has evolved, what questions its practitioners grapple with today, and what the framework contributes—as well as where its limits lie—in understanding political life. Organized into five modules, the course examines the field’s origins and boundaries; anthropological perspectives on politics and the political; debates around the nation, state, public sphere, and civil society; anthropological approaches to protest and revolution; and ethnographies of political violence.

Is nature the external world; or are humans part of nature? Is human subjectivity natural; or is it socially constructed? Are relations between human and non-human animals, or actors, social? Is there a pristine nature out there? Such debates around ‘the social construction of 'nature’ have animated discussions of the relationship between nature and society since at least the late twentieth century, and continue to offer valuable insights. This course introduces students to these debates around the perceptions of nature—human, non-human and more-than-human; the historical and often unsuccessful disciplining of more-than-human natures by dominant social, political and economic interests; and the emancipatory and democratic politics for socioecological justice that counter capitalogenic expropriations of more-than-human natures.
The first module examines the binary distinction between human and non-human nature, including human and non-human animals. In the second module we discuss the disciplining of more-than-human natures (including other species and affordances such as land, rivers or forests) by historically particular dominant interests. A fieldtrip animates the discussions in this module through exposure to lived negotiations of socioecological relations in a particular setting. The third module discusses the historical subjection of more-than-human natures to market imperatives in the pursuit of profits, and how their exploitation, depletion and dispossession have accelerated multiple socioecological crises in what has been termed the capitalocene. We end with a discussion of what democratic and emancipatory politics of more-than-human justice might look like.

column6: Humiliation: Power, Subjectivity, and Social Life
column19: This course explores humiliation as both an intimate emotion and a powerful social force. Drawing on philosophy, psychoanalysis, ethnography, military and conflict studies, caste/race scholarship, and literature—with South Asia as a comparative anchor—students examine humiliation as a moral violation, psychological injury, tool of governance, structural condition, and literary motif. The course equips students with theoretical insight, ethnographic sensitivity, and ethical reflexivity while engaging with challenging histories and lived experiences.

column6: Sociology and STS through Science Fiction
column19:
Sociology and STS Through Science Fiction” treats speculative cinema and short fiction as the basis for a comparative ethnography of power. Across eleven weeks, the course follows a curated sequence of science fiction films (Gattaca, Arrival, Akira, Blade Runner, Snowpiercer, Equilibrium, The Matrix, District 9, Sorry to Bother You, Brazil) alongside anti-caste and South Asian speculative writing drawn primarily from The Blaft Book of Anti-Caste SF and The Gollancz Book of South Asian Science Fiction, Volume 2. These materials provide grounded, situated imaginaries of genetic citizenship, infrastructural domination, border regimes, racial capitalism, bureaucratic violence, and abolitionist horizons that are often only abstractly theorized in canonical social theory. Students thus learn to read films/speculative narratives as sites where states, markets, and technical systems are made visible: how metrics fabricate “valid” and “invalid” lives; how simulations and media infrastructures encode ideology; how camps, checkpoints, databases, and documents enact caste/race, gender, and class hierarchies; how insurgent publics, underground networks, and counter-futures contest these arrangements. Social Media & Society" examines digital platforms as central institutions of contemporary social life. Rather than treating social media as a discrete technological domain, the course conceptualizes platforms as sociotechnical
infrastructures that mediate visibility, labor, identity, governance, and inequality at scale. The course begins by analyzing the infrastructural and classificatory foundations of social networking systems before progressing to the forms of work, algorithmic reasoning, and public-making that they enable. Subsequent modules address the intensification of harm—misogyny, racism, casteism, extremism—as well as the emergence of illicit economies, trauma narratives, and new forms of digital care. The syllabus combines foundational scholarship in Sociology, STS, and Media Studies with recent qualitative and theoretical studies from diverse global contexts.
Across these readings, students engage with influencers, platform workers, nationalist publics, disability activists, sex workers, extremist groups, and content moderators—each case illustrating how platform architectures and governance regimes shape social practices and political possibilities. By the end of this course, students will be able to articulate how social media systems structure contemporary social life and to critically assess the political, ethical, and epistemic implications of their design and governance.

column6: Social Conflict and Religious Division: Exploring Contemporary India
column19:
How do food practices and taboos perpetuate caste,
racial, and religious divisions in India? In what ways has forced assimilation impacted the cultural and political autonomy of Indigenous communities? What gendered insights emerge from the lived experiences of half-widows in Kashmir in the context of prolonged conflict? Can religious violence be understood as a catalyst for political mobilization and state consolidation in contemporary India?
How does religious polarization shape diasporic politics? Does popular culture in India sustain majoritarian worldviews and contribute to their normalization? To what extent does digital media amplify political and social divisions? How does Bollywood cinema, as a popular culture, intensify stereotypes and othering? This course critically interrogates key questions at the intersection of politics, history, society, and culture in contemporary India. Structured around three interrelated units, Unframing India, Politics of Popular Culture and India in Cinema, the course traces the historical and political trajectories that have shaped the nation’s cultural and ideological formation.

This introductory and interdisciplinary course focuses on human/animal stories to explore socio-cultural worldviews especially in relation to identity, social justice and the redistribution of natural resources, particularly in South Asia. Through ethnographies, films, novels and paintings we will explore the lives of those living in communities which depend on or live close to wild animals. The course aims to be an informative, provocative and a fun introduction to an exciting and relatively new field of scholarship.

column6: Global Mobilities: Borders, Ecology, and Development
column19:
This course offers readings to understand the dynamics of human mobility across the globe, with a particular focus on borders, ecological change, and development-induced displacement. Drawing on interdisciplinary studies, the course is a sociological and anthropological exploration of mobility, whether by force, necessity, or aspiration, in a world increasingly shaped by border security, ecological crises, geopolitical conflicts, and economic development initiatives. One major theme will be the changing nature of borders and how state policies, international regimes, and border technologies mediate mobility, often creating new forms of exclusion and precarity. The second major focus of the course will address ecological displacement—mobility triggered by climate change, environmental degradation, and natural disasters. Students will examine how environmental stressors intersect with existing vulnerabilities, including race, class, gender, and indigeneity, creating complex patterns of mobility and immobility. The third focus will be on development-induced displacement: the forced relocation of communities due to infrastructure projects, urban expansion, resource extraction, and conservation initiatives. Students will analyse the underlying logics of such displacement, often justified by narratives of progress or national interest, and the uneven power relations that shape who gets displaced, who benefits, and who is left behind.

The course, though borrowing readings from all disciplines, is grounded in anthropology as it connects the everyday experience of migration from across the world with questions of power. These are just some of the questions we will ask ourselves throughout the course as students will be encouraged to reflect on the assumptions and concepts that underlie our often strongly held beliefs about migration.

column6: Quantitative Research Methods in Humanities and Social Sciences
column19: This course will introduce students to research methods in the humanities and social sciences. This is designed as a foundational course for those interested in research in the humanities and social sciences. It is meant to familiarize students with a broad range of methods and analytical tools commonly employed in research in these fields.
A theoretical and close encounter with major Indian socio-political postcolonial movements , using film, memoir and text.

Clay working, instrument making, rhythm, and music have been part of human craft and culture since even before the formation of civil societies. From China to Peru, in every ancient culture around the world, clay flutes or ocarinas, clay horns or water whistles, or some other form of musical instrument, have all used the innate resonant quality of fired clay or the space that it contains, to produce musical notes and specific sounds.
This practical, hands-on course will start off by introducing students to the basic techniques of working with clay and making hollow forms by hand. Once students have a grasp of the fundamentals, they will explore and create musical instruments, as well as forms that amplify sound, both in the fired as well as the unfired stage of the clay. 
As a complement to hands-on work with clay, students will also study some of the forms and simple instruments in a range of ancient as well as modern cultures around the world through readings, research, videos, and guest lectures.
By the end of the course, students will be encouraged to experiment with creating and attempting to play their own wind, percussion, or string instruments with clay.

column6: Documentary Film Documentary Film-Making in the Times of Crisis
column19: This course provides a comprehensive understanding of the critical role that independent documentary filmmakers play in portraying and questioning India's complex socio-political landscape and offers practitioner’s insights and insider information on the realities on the ground about independent documentary film making. From decoding ideologies, knowing the nuances of identifying, approaching and filming sensitive subjects and navigating dangerous terrains while on the field to shoot, such as riots and andolans, the lens of the filmmaker becomes the unsettling truth teller of immutable visuals, facts and footage. How to negotiate between critical aesthetics and practical questions of safety, security, permissions and ethical concerns, will be taught in this course. Students will explore the breadth of documentary film maker’s daring journeys and documentary films/ raw footages and archives as the crucible of the times we live in, be it the Emergency, Delhi Riots or CAA protests. The crux of the course is how much truth can one tell in a climate of censorship and how?

column19: Art Technologies and Design is an art technologies course introducing technical skills and proficiencies that equip students to participate in the ever-growing digital and multidisciplinary arts practices. In this iteration, we will discuss current trends in the fields of digital media design, sound art and communication. The course will focus on the philosophy of sound and listening, introducing students to industry-valued production practices in sound design for film and experimental mediums. The course will encourage learners to collaborate and innovate, based on their interests and experiment with professional technologies, be it hardware equipment or software. Through small-scale projects students will learn methods of recording sounds, manipulating them and stitching audio-visual narratives. Students interested in music will also be able to understand how to strike the right balance between sound design and backgrounds score in narratives.

column6: Philosophical, Aesthetic, and Social Dimensions in Bhakti: An Introduction
column19:
This course offers an interdisciplinary exploration of the tradition of Bhakti as an embodied practice of attention, to understand one’s relation with self, the divine, and the world. Through close readings of poetry, song, and performance across diverse Bhakti traditions (translated and in original wherever available), students will learn how to listen to various shades of expression of bhakti and what it implies; ultimately reaching an understanding that devotion, indeed, is an inadequate translation of it.
The course explores regional and vernacular Bhakti traditions through the voices of female saints like Meera, Andal, Akka Mahadevi, and Janabai. Listening to their poetry and songs in class will help students reflect on love, desire, and the subversion of social and gender norms. We then turn to Nirgun (Formless) Bhakti and the radical critiques of Kabir and Ravidas, examining their challenges to caste, ritualism, and hypocrisy, and their vision of an anti-caste world. Listening becomes a critical mode of engaging with Bhakti across its diverse textual and performance contexts. The course concludes with the introspective poetry of Lalla Ded (Lalla) of Kashmir and the living musical tradition of the Bauls of Bengal.
Drawing from religious studies, literary studies, ethnomusicology, gender studies, the course uses poetry, song, performance recordings, live performances, and films to facilitate a participatory understanding of Bhakti. Students will listen, participate in singing, read, and reflect not only on texts and performance, but also on the sensory and affective worlds they create.

Over this term we will take our first steps in creative writing. To become a writer of prose fiction you must be able to do at least three things well: read, write and edit. In this class we will engage significantly with each of these practices. Many people enjoy writing, but if you are not prepared to read deeply and extensively you cannot be a good writer, and your work will not develop as it should in this class. The term is divided into three modules, each pertaining to a fundamental aspect of writing fiction: Person, Plot, Place. We will explore what these are and how they relate to the work you hope to finally produce. Every week we will read the work of accomplished prose writers of the past decades and try and understand how their writing illuminates the concepts we have just covered.

Much of the appeal of William Shakespeare’s seemingly inexhaustible power as a playwright lies in some of the most astonishing adaptations of his plays. This course will discuss how his plays have travelled across culture and medium, regions and most importantly, languages; and how the inherent potency of a Shakespearean play is unlocked in tongues far removed from the original. By bringing together some of his most well- known plays to stand in comparison with some of the most interesting and landmark cinematic adaptations, the course hopes to highlight both older and newer issues that have surfaced in Shakespearean studies over the years: from honour, state, authority, ambition, filial love, jealousy and madness to the more recent explorations of race, culture, sexuality, identity, gender and authorship itself. Also, the course would want to understand the politics and poetics of adaptation, elemental film theory and f ilm form, the language of cinema and how iconic texts perform as visual imagery. The primary focus of the course are four of Shakespeare’s most canonical works: Macbeth, Hamlet, King Lear and Julius Caesar. Having said that, the course will immediately get into challenging the very idea of their canonicity by entering them into a productive encounter with their cinematic adaptations. These adaptations, some of which will be studied closely, not only reinterpret these much revered literary classics, but also tend to push them away from having an ontological centre. To that end, the course is equally a study of how literary texts are both iconised and destabilized by the image.

column19: This course aims to introduce concepts such as literary “periods,” “movements,” or “influences” as a fundamental instrument of criticism, enabling scholars to understand, by way of comparison or contrast, innovations in form and genre that go beyond the particular practices of individual writers. Focussing on a specific literary movement—English Romanticism of the nineteenth century—we will examine what a periodising approach to literary studies looks like: When and how is a literary or artistic movement born, named, periodised, and canonised? And what does organising texts and writers into particular movements or periods do to the way in which we read them? The course will then make a distinction between historical periods and literary or artistic movements, the latter being defined, not merely chronologically, but in terms of specific literary and artistic goals shared across time, place, mediums, and genres. We will regard the movement in question as defined by critics retrospectively, as well as by the members themselves. And finally we will read Romanticism in relation to movements that preceded and succeeded it, as a way to gain insight into how movements fit into a historical continuum, how some movements are distinct and well defined while others are more nebulous and fluid, and why the notion of movements has at times been a point of contention among scholars.

This course is a deep dive into the reading and practice of poetry. What is a poem? How is it fashioned? What makes it such a powerful form of literary enchantment? This course explores the building blocks of poetry, interspersed with readings of poems from around the world – canonical and less familiar. As it delves into questions around the role of sound and metaphor, free verse and fixed form, inspiration and craft, it will examine how we might become better practitioners, as well as better listeners. The course will combine immersive practice sessions with readings, group discussions with one-on-one interactions. In addition to multiple writing and reading exercises, students will turn in a final assignment that includes six rigorously-workshopped poem drafts and one poem review.

This course will engage significantly with a specific form of creative fiction writing: speculative fiction. It will be one of a rotating series of Genre courses that we hope to offer as part of the Creative Writing minor. Speculative fiction is an extremely popular genre among writers and students. At the outset of this course, we will engage with a fundamental question: What makes a piece of writing speculative? As the term progresses, we will look deeply at the most popular forms of speculative fiction: dystopic literature, fantasy writing and alternate history fiction. Students will work on short pieces during the first weeks, and then are expected to develop and complete a longer story by the end of term.

column6: Reading Aesthetics, Writing Modernity: Sanskrit Poetics and Indian Literature
column19: This course is for literature and philosophy students and bridges classical Indian aesthetic theory (Sanskrit and philosophy) with modern literary and comparative theory (vernacular, global, and historical frameworks) to trace the continuities, transformations, and re-framings of Indian aesthetic concepts across time and languages. The first half of the course traces the historical development of aesthetic and literary theorization in the Indian context. The discussion relies on two of the major schools of Sanskrit poetics– the Rasa school of Bharata and the Dhvani school of Ānandavardhana. It will shed light on how Indian aesthetic thought shifted from performance to language and from expression to interpretation. This section concludes with discussing how modern Indian philosophers revisited classical theories and reinterpreted them for the modern reader. In the second half of the course, the goal is to explore how modern Indian literary thinkers connected literary history, vernacular modernity, and the classical past. We will discuss moments of nationalist transformation and recasting of the Sanskritic tradition, questions of comparativism between languages, and the emergence of counter-cultural stances that query the hegemony of a singular tradition. How did writers, critics, and philosophers create bridges between the śāstraic and the modern, between kāvya and sāhitya?

column6: The Body in Medieval and Early Modern Europe
column19: Visceral, often uncontrolled and in states of excess or restraint, the body confounds the imagination, transforming and transmuting as it moves through the world. It consumes and is consumed, and is an infinitely malleable entity. The Medieval and Early Modern periods reimagined the relationship between bodies— political, philosophical, spiritual, social and aesthetic— articulating new possibilities for the ways in which bodies manifested themselves and their own positioning within a larger world; one opened up by trade, travel and encounter. In this course, we will explore different understandings and expressions of the body, embodiment, and corporeal subjectivity in European literature from the 6th through 18th centuries. Designed to be interdisciplinary, the course examines discourses of the body and its relationship to questions of biological, chronological, ontological, and epistemic subjectivity. Scholars including Peter Stallybrass and Stephen Greenblatt, have placed the genesis of modern ideas of embodied subjectivity in the early modern period, while Geraldine Heng, JRR Tolkien, Harold Bloom, and others, have theorized the importance of examining medieval discourses of embodiment as precursors to contemporary understandings of race, gender, disability, monstrosity and more. This course draws together scholarship from across disciplines– history, art history, literary studies, performance studies, disability studies, and critical period studies, to complicate, enrich, and diversify how the body becomes and is a site of interrogation and inquiry in the humanities and humanistic social sciences. The course structure is driven by its primary texts, which will change in every iteration. The current iteration of the course focuses on performance and expressive culture, primarily drawn from the Western European canon. Primary readings include Beowulf, the lais of Marie de France, and theatrical texts by Shakespeare, Corneille, and Moliere.

column19: This interdisciplinary research-led module explores the cartographical South – from e.g., the port cities of Cape Town, Durban, Chennai, Adelaide and Sydney to the islands of Sri Lanka, Zanzibar and Mauritius. These transoceanic southern spaces are also transhemispheric, so what might be the continuities and connections geographically between southern sites on different latitudinal lines? Sri Lankan historian Sujit Sivasundaram’s marvellous monographs, Islanded and Waves Across the South, suggest more navigational and narrative strategies for conceptualising and rethinking what we count as archives, and what we call the ‘South’. Our goal in this module is indeed visual, archival and cartographical, as we travel across novels, maps, photographs and other materials to register coordinates on coastlines and seascapes. The texts also take us into the heart of the country, e.g., to the interior landscapes of Namaqualand, the Karoo, Flinders Ranges, Pulicat Lake, Yala National Park, and the botanical gardens of Kandy, Kirstenbosch and Kew. Examining the legacies of the ‘networks of empire’ that bring many of these sites and texts together historically and geographically, the module is excellent preparation for further interdisciplinary research on South-South mobilities, and asks questions about colonial legacies, ideas of ownership, belonging, cultural identity, and migration. The current variation of this module, first launched at SOAS in 2014, is inspired by a series of events: the travelling exhibition, Scenes from the South that I curated in collaboration with universities and museums (2020; 2022; 2024); the public programme, ‘Speaking from the South’ at the University of Adelaide in 2024 that was inspired by this work; the Cátedra Coetzee Literatures of the South programme from 2015-2018 at UNSAM in Argentina, led by Nobel Prizewinner J. M. Coetzee; and the crucial forerunner of my more recent research, a 1992 University of London conference, ‘Southern Spaces’, from which the module takes its name.
