This course will equip students broadly interested in the biological sciences and allied disciplines to develop fundamental skills for managing, exploring and analysing data, and interpreting and communicating findings. The course provides a hands-on learning experience using data from multiple fields of study to master basic statistical tools widely used in the discipline and become familiar with the range of advanced quantitative tools to inform avenues for further specialization. In addition to imparting skills to quantify single variables and relationships between multiple variables, the course will use real-world datasets to help students learn how to deal with noisy data, uncertainty of findings and ethical concerns that are common to the discipline

From classical to molecular genetics, this course seeks to provide a close understanding of the processes involved in heredity, and begins with the fundamental principles of inheritance as determined by Mendel. In this context, we study the chemical nature, physico-chemical structure, and replication and recombination of DNA. The histone code and epigenetic methods of inheritance will be considered, as will the translation of genetic information into regulatory RNA or structural or functional protein. The elucidation of the genetic code and the mechanism and regulation of gene action, such as in the operon model are investigated alongside processes of extrachromosomal inheritance.

The course will bring together various topics in Genetics and Advanced Cell Biology. The portion on genetics will include procedures and experiments using the fruit-fly Drosophila melanogaster as the model organism, for instance the observation of wild type and mutant characteristics using the compound and stereo microscopes, the culture of Drosophila, the longitudinal observation of their life-cycles, the proper and meticulous use of a lab notebook/ journal, computational exercises in phylogeny, and, time permitting, recombinant DNA techniques. The Advanced Cell Biology course will include procedures for nucleic acid analysis including nucleic acid extraction, chromatography, and quantitative PCR, and for protein analysis by chromatography.

In this course, we examine biological systems through the lenses of anatomy (structure) and physiology (function), that make life possible across scales of complexity - from the simplest forms to the most intricate. Through this approach, all courses that we have encountered so far will be considered in establishing how we can begin to comprehend what life, in a biological sense, means. Apart from such familiar systems as encountered in school (the digestive, respiratory, circulatory, excretory, nervous and reproductive, for instance), we explore concepts like homoeostasis and thermoregulation

column6: Ways of Knowing: Methods and Communication
column19: This offering, the other of a two-part course, will use a seminar-style format to expose students to literature in the biological sciences to serve three important and interconnected purposes. The selected pieces of work will expose students to forms of inquiry used in the biological sciences to produce new knowledge and to advance the discipline. Students will also learn multiple types of communication in the discipline. Finally, students will learn to assess critically the work and findings reported in the primary literature. The course will bridge the gap between simplified concepts in standard biology textbooks and the rigour, complexity and uncertainty of findings in the primary literature, including, among others, journals and theses.
column21: Students need to successfully complete it in their 3rd year to be eligible for a capstone project in their 4th year.

column19: We are living in what many consider to be a unique period of time in the history of planet Earth, the Anthropocene era, wherein humans are modifying Earth’s environment through myriad pathways, including the burning of fossil fuels, overexploitation of natural resources and large-scale changes in patterns of land-use. These changes have major consequences for ecological systems at multiple levels of biological organization from the individual and population to the community and ecosystem. This course will not only focus on the mechanisms through which humans are altering the air, water and land of planet Earth, but also to apply concepts from ecological and evolutionary biology theory to understand how these changes are likely to impact life on Earth. Students will learn to critically evaluate the primary scientific literature related to the field of global change biology, and also to address specific questions through the graphical and/or statistical analyses of real-world data. The course will pay particular attention to the most critical crises associated with anthropogenic global change, and also on how these changes can impact health and well-being of humans through various mechanisms ranging from reduced access to ecosystem services (e.g., clean air and water) to the increased risk of emergence of novel diseases (e.g., COVID-19).

This is a seminar course where we will discuss and analyze research papers, and solve problems as assignments, and there will be presentations of the papers.  
Proteins are fascinating molecular machines that carry out every function inside the cells whose properties are so useful that we employ them as therapeutic agents, catalysts, and materials. Many diseases stem from protein mutations impairing their folding, structure, or activity. This course will discuss the physical chemistry of protein molecules. This course is for students of Biological Sciences who are comfortable with mathematics. This is also a course for chemistry and physics students who want to think about proteins.

This course examines the psychological, biological, biomedical, and sociotechnical dimensions of self-tracking practices in contemporary digital life. With a central focus on the biological and cognitive mechanisms underlying self-regulation, feedback, and sense-making, the course explores how digital technologies enable a prospective approach to health management, and how they mediate and reshape attention, decision-making, memory, emotion, and embodied experience; the course also  Drawing on perspectives from biology, cognitive neuroscience, behavioral psychology, and cultural theory, students will critically engage with topics such as neurofeedback, affective computing, persuasive design, and the cognitive labor of managing personal data. The course also addresses broader social and ethical implications, including surveillance, inequality, and the politics of measurement. Through interdisciplinary readings and experiential assignments, students will investigate how cognitive processes are both reflected in and transformed by the quantified self.

This course introduces the physical chemistry of biological systems. The topics include an introduction to the basics of statistical mechanics to understand the connections between macroscopic thermodynamic properties and microscopic molecular properties, chemical potentials, equilibrium states, binding cooperativity, behaviour of macromolecules in solution and at the interfaces, and solvation. We will
discuss protein structure, genomic analysis, single-molecule biomechanics, and biomaterials. To foster a deeper appreciation of the empirical aspects of the discipline, we will discuss Nuclear Magnetic Resonance measurements and provide practical demonstrations using the NMR spectrometer at Krea University. We will also discuss the recent developments in the use of Artificial Intelligence in
solving really hard Biophysics problems of understanding protein structure and dynamics. We will implement the computation of protein structure for practical sessions.

This course explores the darker side of scientific research — the deliberate falsification, fabrication, and plagiarism that have led to the retraction of biomedical research papers. Through a series of case studies, students will investigate how misconduct was detected, how it propagated through the literature, the consequences for the individuals and institutions involved, and the broader implications for scientific credibility. The course also examines systemic pressures that foster misconduct and the evolving safeguards implemented by journals, funding agencies, and institutions.

column17: Guha Dharmarajan , Gautam Banerjee , Kalyan Chakrabarti , Lakshman Varanasi , Shivani Jadeja , Shyam Kumar Sudhakar , Sivakumar Srinivasan , Vaishali Sharma , Yadugiri Tiruvaimozhi
column19:
Welcome to an exhilarating journey through modern biology—a discipline that sits at the intersection of every major field of human inquiry. This course will take you on a dynamic exploration of life's interconnectedness and the innovative ways we study it. Beginning with life's origins and evolutionary foundations, we'll traverse scales from molecules to ecosystems, discovering how biology interfaces with various fields ranging from physics and chemistry to psychology and data science. Each module showcases cutting-edge research and real-world applications, such as CRISPR gene editing, AI-powered drug design and pandemic preparedness. Focusing on interdisciplinary thinking, through this course you will see how physics has helped decode photosynthesis at quantum scales, how machine learning revolutionizes protein structure prediction, and how systems biology integrates vast datasets to understand complex diseases. A hands-on laboratory tour midway through the course brings these concepts to life, while modules on global change biology and epidemiology demonstrate biology's critical role in addressing humanity's most pressing challenges. The course culminates in collaborative presentations where you'll envision "Biology X"—the next frontier of biological discovery that excites you most.
Whether you're considering biology as a major, exploring it as a complement to another discipline, or simply curious about how life works, this course reveals the extraordinary career possibilities at biology's rapidly expanding frontiers. From biotechnology startups to conservation initiatives, from computational biology to public health—the skills and perspectives you'll gain in biology are increasingly valuable across sectors.

The course will introduce the students to the basic concepts of chemistry accompanied by experimental demonstrations in class. This course is aimed at providing the necessary fundamental knowledge and methodology for the further study of chemistry and biology. Emphasis will be placed more towards understanding the concepts rather than just going through the various theories.

Spectroscopic techniques play a very important role in science and technology. It is important to understand these methods to know their advantages, applicability and limitations.  Spectroscopy plays a pivotal role in our understanding of matter, energy and their interaction; in addition, it also plays a very important role in materials characterization. A few non-spectroscopic methods will also be discussed in this course. This course will cover the principles and application of the various experimental methods and basic instrumentation.

The students will develop proficiency in using various laboratory
equipment and techniques that are required for chemistry students. Student’s will perform various types of experiments (acid-base titration, redox titration, complexometric experiment, basic spectroscopic experiment)

A detailed study of how organic reactions occur, emphasizing structure–reactivity relationships, energy profiles, acidity/basicity, isotope effects, catalysis, and the role of electronic, steric, and solvent effects in determining reaction pathways.

Coordination Chemistry is the study of the transition metals vis-à-vis their periodic properties, the compounds they form and their chemical reactivity. This course will also serve as an introduction to Bio-inorganic Chemistry

This course acquaints students with all basic organic laboratory procedures, presented in three major parts: (1) Techniques in organic chemistry laboratory, (2) Single-step organic synthesis, and (3) Organic qualitative analysis. 
The techniques section acquaints the students with standard techniques such as recrystallization, extraction, distillation, thin-layer chromatography, and column chromatography. Also, the techniques section has a relatively simple illustrative experiment with each. The synthesis section involves experiments related to simple reactions such as nitration, halogenation, esterification, etc. The Organic Qualitative Analysis section involves the characterization and/or identification of various organic compounds. In this section, students study and perform the characteristic chemical reactions of organic functional groups

Spectroscopic characterization of molecules and materials. This course builds upon the fundamentals the student learned in CHEM216 and provides practical usage of key spectroscopic tools to identify various materials. Following a brief recap of the key principles covered in CHEM216, the course will extensively cover the use of infrared spectroscopy, mass spectrometry, nuclear magnetic spectroscopy, and ultraviolet spectroscopy for the structural elucidation of various materials.

The Cheminformatics course aims to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the principles, techniques, and applications of cheminformatics in drug discovery, materials science, and other related fields. Students will learn how to apply computational and informatics methods to solve chemical problems, analyze large-scale chemical data, and design new molecules with desired properties.
This course is designed for students who would like to pursue their careers in industrial research (pharma, chemical, and materials) and higher studies in the future. Therefore the course has a few hours of hands on. The biology, chemistry, and computer science students will significantly benefit from this course as it will complement their knowledge of the informatics of chemicals.

This laboratory course introduces students to programming and computational tools used to study chemical systems. Using sofwtares like Gromacs and gaussian and standard computational chemistry packages, students learn to perform molecular modeling, visualize structures, analyze simulation data, and interpret computational results.

A deeper examination of modern inorganic chemistry, covering ligand field theory, reaction mechanisms of coordination complexes, metal–ligand bonding, organometallic catalysis, and the electronic structure of transition-metal compounds. Students analyze how electronic and geometric factors govern stability and reactivity.

This course provides a comprehensive exploration of systems through systems programming in C, delving into the intricate workings of processors, memory subsystems, and program execution. We will examine the process of compiling C programs into machine-level instructions, gaining insights into compiler mechanics and code optimization techniques. Throughout the journey, students will acquire invaluable skills for developing secure, reliable programs that leverage computing resources effectively.
column20: Software Design Practical and Principles of Computer Systems

column19:
Algorithms are unambiguous instructions for solving problems. From a utilitarian perspective, efficient use of computer machinery is both desirable and necessary. One of the key concerns regarding efficiency in computing is the time taken by a computing machine to run an algorithm. This course introduces some general principles and guidelines which enable designing faster algorithms for a wide range of computational problems.
 
 Learning Outcomes include:
 Learn to distinguish slow algorithms from faster ones by quantifying the amount of time taken by an algorithm to solve a problem through asymptotic analysis.
 A view of the general
 paradigms used for solving a problem, and an 
 overview of basic complexity classes.
 Prove the correctness of an algorithm, and do a runtime analysis.
 Ability to abstract computational tasks, and applying algorithmic techniques towards problem solving.
column20: Software Design Practical and Introduction to Machine Learning

column19: Principles of Programming Languages is a deep dive into analytical foundations of programming languages, their design, and implementation. These foundations have proved to be of enduring importance, and hold the key to understanding future developments in programming languages. These foundations are centered around the semantics of program elements, which reflect how program elements are interpreted as a program is executed. This course will use interpretation of programs as the approach to learn these principles - a “mental model” - of programming languages. It will draw on the PLAI (“Programming Languages: Application and Interpretation”) body of material and will be taught using Racket, a dialect of Scheme. In this course, “language” does not refer to “surface structure”, also known as “syntax”, but will focus on the “semantics” or meaning of programs
column20: Principles of Programming I and Principles of Programming II. Functional programming course will be a plus, but is not strictly required

column19: It is imperative for any graduate of computer science to understand the formal definition of computation, and the possibilities and limits of computing. Moreover, any distinction between decidability and undecidability needs a good mathematical model of computers and computation. This course introduces the powerful idea of mathematical models to analyse computation, and the nature of the relationship between formal languages, logic and machines. This course introduces the classical mathematical models used to analyse computation, including finite state automata, grammars, and Turing Machines.

This course introduces students to the concept of high performance computing (HPC). Students will be taught the fundamentals of HPC and the techniques to solve numerical/programming problems where performance is critical.

Social choice theory is the study of aggregating individual preferences. One of the
 immediate applications is voting: how to aggregate each individual’s choice into a
 collective choice. In the recently concluded New York City mayoral elections, voters ranked the
 candidates. On the other hand, in the upcoming Bihar elections, voters will choose
 their favourite candidate. Which system is fairer? Social choice, however, is not just restricted to voting but to welfare economics in general where the state has to distribute welfare in a way that maximises public satisfaction. In this course, we will look at social choice from a computation lens. We will contemplate on the consequences of theoretical results and provide
 computational safeguards to manipulation tactics like bribery.

This course provides comprehensive knowledge of implementing quantum
 algorithms using Qiskit. Qiskit has been an integral part of practical quantum
 computing. A key component of the course is implementing known quantum
 algorithms in using IBM Qiskit, understanding various challenges due to the effect of
 noise and methods to mitigate them.

This course provides a hands-on introduction to Natural Language Processing (NLP), blending practical applications with core theoretical concepts. It covers essential lexical and semantic operations such as text normalization and word embeddings, along with standard metrics for measuring content similarity, text classification techniques, and methods for modeling context and meaning in language data. The course concludes with an accessible introduction to the practice and theory of Transformers and Large Language Models (LLMs).
 Throughout, the focus will be on implementing the concepts discussed in class. Students will work with leading NLP libraries including SpaCy, NLTK, and Scikit-learn. By the end of the course, they will have gained both practical skills and a solid theoretical foundation, preparing them for advanced study or professional roles in NLP.

column19:
This beginner-level deep learning course is
 designed for 3rd- and 4th-year students and can also serve as a fresh
 introduction to modern machine learning. It provides a thorough
 foundation in core concepts by beginning with classical methods such as
 regression and classification, and then building naturally towards shallow
 and deep neural networks.
 The course begins with regression through a simple curve-fitting
 example, introducing key ideas such as error functions, regularization,
 and the bias–variance trade-off. Regression and classification are then
 presented as single-layer networks, highlighting linear models,
 discriminant functions, and generative vs. discriminative classifiers.
 
 These methods motivate the shift from fixed basis functions to learning
 representations directly from data, naturally leading to neural networks.
 Students are then introduced to deep neural networks, with a focus on
 gradient descent, backpropagation, and regularization. The course
 concludes with an introduction to Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)
 and their practical applications
column20: For further Deep Learning based electives

column19:
This course will provide a rigorous introduction to elementary data structures and their
 analysis and applications to various computational problems in computer science. In addition, this course
 will introduce students to key algorithmic techniques for design and analysis of data structures for various
 problems that arise in the field of computer science. The course provides a broad overview of fundamental
 concepts involved in the design of algorithms and their complexity analysis.

This course provides an overview of the following topics: Calculus (Limits, Continuity, Basic
 Overview of Differential and Integral Calculus with Applications that involve modelling, and Differential
 Equations). Multivariable Calculus: Derivatives, partial derivatives, differentiation with respect to a vector;
 gradient, Hessian, Jacobian. Taylor's theorem in 1 and n dimensions, with Lagrange remainder.
 Optimization in 1 and n dimensions, classification of stationary points. Constrained optimization and the
 method of Lagrange multipliers.

This course will introduce the students to (i) Elements of Programming (variables,
 assignments, built-in data types, conditionals, loops, arrays, input-output processing; (ii) Functions and
 Modules; (iii) Object-Oriented programming; and (iv) basic algorithms and data structures (data frames,
 dictionary, list, tuples, etc) for sorting and searching. This course will also introduce the students to a
 collection of open-source tools that are required to analyse data and solve data science problems including
 pandas, NumPy, and matplotlib, and seaborn.

The course essentially is a hands-on introduction to various types of neural networks used in  machine learning and decision trees. Topics include Decision Trees, Bagging Random Forests and Boosting,  Introduction to Basic Neural Networks, Activation Functions, Deep Neural Networks (Convolutional Neural  Networks (CNN), Recurrent Neural Networks (LSTM), Autoencoders, Generative Adversarial Networks  (GAN), and transformer architectures with applications to problems in Image Processing and Computer  Vision. This course will also introduce Python tools and libraries including scikit-learn, Keras, TensorFlow,  and PyTorch.

This course provides a comprehensive introduction to Natural Language Processing
 (NLP), covering foundational concepts, classical machine learning techniques, and
 modern deep learning architectures. Students will learn practical methods for text
 preprocessing, feature extraction, and building NLP models for applications like text
 classification, translation, and summarization. The course also explores real-world
 applications of NLP in domains such as finance, cybersecurity, and healthcare,
 equipping learners with skills to implement and evaluate advanced NLP systems

column17: Balasubramanian Gopalswamy, Srinivasan Kalyanasundaram and Somasundaram
column19: The Financial Analytics course is designed to provide students with the analytical skills and techniques necessary to navigate the complex world of financial markets, investment strategies, and corporate finance. The course focuses on integrating quantitative methods and data-driven insights into financial decision-making processes. Through a combination of financial theory, modelling techniques, and hands-on analytical applications, students will develop a strong foundation in financial modelling, portfolio optimization, risk analysis, derivatives trading, and technical analysis. The course will enable students to use descriptive analytics to summarize financial data, prescriptive analytics to optimize investment strategies, and predictive analytics to forecast market trends and price movements.

Cryptography is the science of designing encryption and decryption algorithms for
 providing secure communication between parties over an insecure channel. In the
 present age, cryptography has gained importance and is widely used in many
 disciplines.
 This is a first course in cryptography, with a focus on the algorithmic foundations of
 real-world cryptosystems, aiming to strike a balance between theory and application.
 In this class, we will cover the basic mathematics necessary to better understand
 various cryptographic protocols, algorithms, and attacks. This will provide a solid
 understanding of the practical issues involved in applying cryptographic techniques
 to design secure systems.
column21:
Prerequisites: Basic programming and mathematical maturity. The course is self-contained,
 covering all mathematical concepts from scratch.

column19:
How does your phone straighten a photograph of a document? How do panorama apps stitch
 multiple images seamlessly? How do self-driving cars understand depth from stereo cameras? This
 course bridges the mathematical foundations from Geometry for Computer Vision I to real-world
 computer vision applications.
 Building on your solid understanding of projective geometry from Course I, you'll learn how cameras
 capture 3D scenes as 2D images and how to reverse this process computationally. Through hands-on
 programming projects, you'll implement the algorithms behind everyday vision applications—from
 document scanning to 3D reconstruction from photos.
 The course balances mathematical understanding with practical implementation. You'll derive key
 algorithms to understand the mathematics, then implement them in Python to see how they work
 on real data. A substantial optimization primer ensures you understand the mathematical
 foundations underlying computer vision algorithms—what is a cost function, how gradient descent
 works, why RANSAC handles outliers.
 
 No advanced mathematics required—just the geometry from DATA239/COMP239, linear algebra,
 basic calculus, and willingness to learn Python. Through weekly programming assignments, you'll
 build proficiency so that by course end, you'll have implemented core algorithms from scratch and
 built a substantial team project suitable for your portfolio.
 This course sets the foundation for understanding both classical geometric computer vision and
 modern learning-based approaches. Whether you're interested in AI, robotics, AR/VR, or just want
 to understand the technology you use daily, this course offers a unique blend of rigorous
 mathematics and hands-on application.

The course will present the concepts and methods of muItivariate analysis to the readers who have read at least one statistics course. The applications of multivariate methods is emphasized. The concepts of matrix algebra are very important. Matrices simplify the presentation of muItivariate techniques. Normal distribution and Regression models are discussed in the multivariate setup. Further, we introduce key concepts like principal component analysis, factor analysis, discriminant analysis and cluster analysis etc., which are quite relevant for data science.

This course offers a comprehensive introduction to C programming, focusing on developing problem-solving skills and a strong understanding of foundational programming concepts. Students will learn to learn to work on different data structures and write structured, efficient, and modular programs using control structures, functions.

The question of ethics is at the core of our relationship with the environment. Do humans as moral agents have a moral obligation towards other living beings and environmental components? Do our moral obligations change knowing that the environment is the only moral subject? How do we define value? Are all values defined solely by reference to ourselves or our kind, or is there a realm of value that extends beyond the human domain? This course illustrates the history of nature-human relationship and the moral and ethical debates that emerge owing to the present dismal state of this relationship. Students learn about various ethical schools that are in place and further gain an in-depth understanding of the necessary ethical debates by comparing and contrasting these ethical viewpoints. After giving exposure to the theoretical underpinnings of environmental ethics, the second half of the course delves into the practice of ethics by charting out the trajectory of the growth of major environmental movements and the major treaties at the global scale. It will delve into present debates concerning resource conflicts, developmental goals, and societal values to locate the role of ethics in the human-environment relationship. With the advent of the discourses on climate change, the ethical response to the environment became an even more conflicted issue. This course ends with addressing the dilemma of the individuals’ vs. institutions' responsibility and the larger effectiveness of ethical actions.

This course introduces various themes in environmental history, taking as its point of departure the beginnings of the formalised movement of the field in Great Britain and the United States of America, and then forging its way across various parts of our globe in what will be in equal parts survey and case study, though with an eye on the Indian subcontinent. Particular attention will be paid to the effects of environmental thinking in the colonial world as well as to contemporary issues, in particular, climate change and conservation. The themes of the course will be suitable to an introductory level approach to the subject such that students will be in a position to make intelligent and thoughtful contributions to a greater environmental consciousness through the work they may undertake in time to come. To this end, projects will be designed using course and supplemental material and with an emphasis on work conducted outside the classroom to be discussed and portrayed within it as final output.

Geographic Information System (GIS) is widely used across sectors for data analysis and
visualization. The GIS software equips the user to understand and analyse complex issues at spatial and temporal scales. This course intends to expose students to the basics of GIS with hands-on training so that students can use these acquired skills in their respective areas of interest.

This course provides a necessary foundation in environmental toxicology, emphasizing
how chemical, physical, and biological agents adversely affect living organisms and
ecosystems. It explores the sources, occurrence, fate, transport, bioaccumulation,
toxicokinetics, and toxic effects of pollutants in air, water, soil, and food systems.
 Students will analyze how environmental changes and pollution contribute to human and
ecological health risks, while developing an understanding of toxicokinetic processes
(absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion) and factors influencing toxicity.
 Through case studies such as the Bhopal gas tragedy, oil spills, and e-waste
contamination, the course connects theory to global environmental health issues. It
concludes with the principles and applications of Environmental Health Risk Assessment,
enabling students to evaluate exposure, hazard, and risk characterization within
environmental contexts.

Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) is an essential tool used to assess the potential impacts of human activities on the environment, including natural habitats and human health. As human populations continue to grow and expand, and natural resources become increasingly scarce, it is critical that we evaluate the environmental impact of our actions to ensure the sustainability of the planet for future generations.

EIAs provide a comprehensive framework for identifying and analyzing potential environmental impacts of proposed activities, such as land use changes, industrial processes, and infrastructure development. By conducting an EIA, we can identify potential impacts and take necessary measures to minimize or mitigate negative impacts, such as air and water pollution, soil erosion, habitat destruction, and loss of biodiversity. In addition, EIAs can also help identify potential risks to human health, such as exposure to hazardous chemicals, pollution, and infectious diseases.

The Environmental Impact Assessment Laboratory Course is designed to provide students with hands-on experience in conducting environmental impact assessments. The course will cover a broad range of topics, including the principles of chemistry, and biology that are relevant to environmental impact assessments. The course will be entirely composed of laboratory experiments that will teach the principles and techniques involved in environmental impact assessments.
column21: Prerequisites: High school science or General chemistry

column6: Alternative Energy on a Finite Planet
column19:
Transition to carbon-free electricity is central to addressing climate change. These are generally solar, wind, hydro and nuclear – often termed ‘renewables’, ‘green’ or ‘sustainable’. The use of such terms conceals the substantial limitations and impacts of these alternative sources of energy. Energy extraction by solar panels and wind turbines (i.e. their efficiency) are inexorably limited by fundamental physics. Their power densities are substantially lower than those of fossil fuel power plants, and therefore require correspondingly larger land areas for installation relative to a fossil fuel plant of equivalent output. Unless the installation is on degraded land, they can cause serious disruption to wildlife habitats and agricultural lands. We have already witnessed the deleterious impacts of large hydro projects in parts of the country, and those of nuclear energy in other parts of the world. The raw materials that alternative energy installations are composed of and constructed from – metal ores, plastics, minerals – are in finite supply. Many are concentrated in certain parts of the world (e.g. Lithium in Chile, Nickel in Indonesia), therefore subject to the vicissitudes of geopolitics (and pandemics). Large solar and wind power farms also substantially affect the microclimate of their installation sites causing local warming. It is also unclear how the vast – and exponentially rising – quantities of spent solar panels and wind turbines that will emerge within the decade can be effectively recycled. The intermittency problems of solar and wind power are well known, and therefore the need for battery technology – with its own land, water, material and chemical footprints. What does all this mean for India’s ambitious alternative energy programme of 500 GW of non-fossil energy by 2030? What will it affect carbon emissions, air pollution, wildlife, agriculture, and human settlements? This course will be a joint exploration of many such questions. 

This is a quantitative course but pitched at high school level of mathematics. The goal of the course, subject to interest and coding skills, is to divide into teams and create maps of India identifying the regions with greatest potential for alternative energy with least impacts – from interwoven science, socio-economic, and ecological perspectives.

column6: Pan Asian Environmentalisms: a short history
column19: This course explores how the various Asian communities that lived along land and maritime trade routes, which linked different parts of Asia, understood the environment and nonhumans. How did the movement of people, as well as the spread of ideas, literature, religions, art, commodities, from pre-modern times to the present, in Asia, shape notions about the nonhuman? How did understandings of the environment rest on religious, medical, cultural and social beliefs?

After a recap of material from Linear Algebra (generalised to arbitrary fields), we will introduce quotients of vector spaces and study their properties. The course then covers a spectrum of foundational material: spaces of linear transformations; duality; determinants; minimal and characteristic polynomials; diagonalisability and triangularisability; inner product spaces; spectral theorems; singular value decompositions; bilinear and sesquilinear forms; Jordan normal forms.

This introductory course is aimed at providing a theoretical foundation in Statistics intending to build a strong quantitative orientation. The course assumes some basic knowledge of calculus and builds on the probability theory course offered in the earlier term. The course is designed to be mathematical (theoretical) in nature and many results and theorems will be derived. The students are expected to learn and implement them primarily using R. Some of these will be covered through assignments.
column21: Students with prior exposure to probability may choose this course.

column6: Proofs and Ideas: An Introduction to Mathematical Thinking
column19: In this course, we will start to think carefully and rigorously about mathematics, mathematical objects, and the idea of proof. We begin with a discussion of the basic mathematical notions of sets, functions, and relations, and proceed to discuss some fundamental properties of the natural numbers and integers. After this foundational background, we will further develop our ability to read, understand, and write proofs through a short study of select mathematical topics. After taking this course, students will have been exposed to the idea of mathematical proof and equipped with the basic tools they will need to study further in the discipline.
column21: This course is a prerequisite for most courses in Mathematics

column19:
This course is an introduction to differential equations from a modern perspective, with a view towards dynamical systems. The course begins with an introduction to the art of modelling real life situations with differential equations: this will help develop an intuition for the subject, and introduce students to the basic ideas behind mathematical modelling. 
 The course will then examine the techniques used to solve differential equations, including qualitative, analytical, and computational techniques. In particular, students will be asked to understand the algorithms that lead to numerical solutions, to interpret the resulting pictures produced by the computer, and to relate these images back to the original application.

This is a first course in Partial Differential Equations for Mathematics students interested in Analysis as well as Applied Mathematics as a discipline. After developing some taxonomy of partial differential equations and mathematical prerequisites, the course will be broadly divided into hyperbolic equations on the one hand and elliptic and parabolic equations on the other. While a broad theory will be developed for first order equations; for second order equations, we will focus on the three prototypes, viz., wave, Laplace and heat equations. An attempt will be made to highlight counterexamples since they drive the theory. Those interested in analysis should get a glimpse of how analysis is the bedrock of all PDEs while those interested in applied math should see how Mathematics can be used to explain physical phenomena.
 
 After completing this course, the students should be equipped with the theoretical tools to analyze first order and second order partial differential equations. They should have a good understanding of first order PDEs and the physical models they represent. They should understand well the three prototype equations – wave, Laplace and heat – that underpin and motivate much of the modern theory of PDEs.

This course is designed to be a concrete introduction to the ideas and methods underlying (differential and integral) calculus of several variables. The emphasis is on examples and computations. The basic techniques from this course are useful in a wide variety of subjects: analysis, probability, (differential) geometry, applied mathematics. This course is designed to be useful for students in both mathematics and areas such as computer science, economics, physics, and data science.
column21:
Multivariable Calculus is intended for second year students. However, first year students who have taken MATH066 and/or did Mathematics in twelfth grade may take this course with explicit permission from the instructor.

column19:
Graph Theory is a central area of discrete mathematics concerned with the study of
 graphs—mathematical structures used to model pairwise relations between objects. This
 course provides a rigorous introduction to the fundamental concepts, results, and methods of
 graph theory, together with selected topics from algebraic graph theory and network
 optimization.
 The course begins with the basic definitions and properties of graphs, including paths, cycles,
 trees, connectivity, and degree sequences. It then develops algorithmic techniques for
 spanning trees, shortest paths, and related optimization problems. The second part introduces
 algebraic tools for studying graphs, including adjacency and Laplacian matrices, eigenvalues,
 eigenvectors, and their interpretations in terms of structure and centrality.
 Building on this foundation, the course explores network flows, duality, and the Max-
 Flow/Min-Cut theorem, along with applications to combinatorial optimization. The final
 module addresses advanced topics such as graph coloring, random graphs, and some more
 algebraic graph theory.
 
 By the end of the course, students will have a clear understanding of the theoretical principles
 underlying modern graph theory and will be able to apply mathematical reasoning to analyze
 and solve problems involving discrete structures and networks.

column17: Tanmoy Chakrabarty, Shivakumar Srinivasan, Venkata Srinu Bhadram, Sushant Raut, Rama Koteswara Rao Kamineni, Nicolas Gheeraert, Aritra Gupta
column19: Physics is fundamental to our comprehension of nature in all its dimensions. But that does not make the discipline scary and dry. In fact, it is fun to discern some of its principles from simple experiments. This course attempts to provide demonstration-based reasoning to learn physics. In particular, we will demonstrate experimentally, discuss and understand concepts such as inertia and mass, friction, energy and its conservation, momentum and its conservation, electric charge and field, conduction of electricity, magnetism, waves and related phenomena. Each class will be devoted to performing an experiment, observation and synthesis of the apt law of nature and a quantitative discussion. This is a 2-credit course and there will be at least ten demonstrations.

Einstein said, “Thermodynamics is the only physical theory of universal content concerning which I am convinced that, within the framework of the applicability of its basic concepts, it will never be overthrown.” That argument is enough to motivate learning thermodynamics. Empirical information gathered over centuries has been consolidated in a few statements called the laws of thermodynamics. In that sense, this subject is also one of the earliest theoretical formulations. Thermodynamics, in particular its nonequilibrium extension, is very important in biological sciences, environmental sciences, climatology and energy studies, to name a few. Entropy, one of the enigmatic notions in physics, was originally formulated by Clausius in the context of heat engines, the objects of study in this subject. A microscopic understanding of thermodynamics is sought in statistical physics. The contributions of greats like Boltzmann and Gibbs still form the foundation of the subject while Jayne’s approach based on information theory is equally important. A brief introduction to these aspects is provided towards the end of the course. Why should one learn this subject? Extension to nonequilibrium systems is still an incomplete program. Of course, significant contributions in recent times include Jarzynsky-Crooks work fluctuation theorems, non-extensive thermodynamics and quantum thermodynamics. The subject is well and alive with unanswered questions.
column20: Statistical Physics (PHYS301), States of matter (PHYS341), Classical Field theory (PHYS401)

column19: Physics is an empirical science. Its conceptual framework is revised to accommodate new empirical evidence from experiments. One of the earliest indications for the need to relook at classical physics was the blackbody emission spectrum. The experimental results were at variance with the prediction of classical physics. Max Planck proposed quantized exchanges of energy between the walls of the blackbody and the radiation within. This resolved the discrepancy between the theoretical predictions and the experimental observations. Einstein proposed quantized energy for the radiation field to explain the photoelectric effect. Bohr proposed non-radiating orbits for electrons to account for the stability of atoms and quantized angular momentum to explain their emissions spectra. All these ad hoc procedures found natural explanations in the quantum theory formulated by Heisenberg and Schrodinger. Their ideas were refined and put on firm scientific footing by Dirac, Pauli, Born, von Neumann, Jordan and others.
column20: Quantyum Physics II (PHYS331), Subatomic Physics (PHYS345), Classical Field theory (PHYS401), States of matter (PHYS341)

column19: In the 18th and 19th centuries, the work of Faraday, Oersted and others showed that the forces of electricity and magnetism can be explained by postulating the existence of a ‘field’ that pervades through space. This field concept allows us to formulate a combined theory of electricity and magnetism called electromagnetism. We will discuss the laws of Coulomb and Gauss in electrostatics and Biot-Savart’s law of magnetism. The properties of these fields in a medium allow us to understand polarization and magnetization of materials. On the theoretical side, these concepts lay the foundation for the first major ‘unification’ of forces in the history of physics – modern theory of electromagnetism.
column20: Classical Physics: Fields II(PHYS225), Classical field theory (PHYS401)

column19: The discovery of radioactivity opened up a whole new realm of physics beyond the classical gravitational and electromagnetic interactions. The properties and structure of the nucleus within an atom, and the forces that bind their constituent protons and neutrons together will be discussed in this course. Using the basic tools of quantum mechanics and special relativity, one can understand the phenomena of alpha, beta and gamma decay, and radioactive transmutations. Even more fundamental than protons and neutrons are the elementary particles -- quarks, leptons and the bosons that mediate interactions between them. Their description as given by the Standard Model of particle physics will be introduced. Finally, the course will discuss detectors and experimental techniques relevant for nuclear and particle physics.

Following from the Electronics course, this elective will discuss the applications of diodes, transistors and integrated circuits like op amps in designing advanced circuits. These have applications not only in the electronics industry but also in measurement and control systems across all fields. Signal amplifiers, analog-to-digital converters, buffer stages, waveform generators and oscillator circuits are some of the circuits that can be constructed. Finally, the course will discuss some digital integrated circuits and their applications which are at the heart of the computer revolution

In this course, we study the wave properties of light such as interference, polarization, and diffraction in more depth. It includes the study of interferometry methods, working principles of diffraction gratings, lasers and holography. Much of it finds applications in photonics, a technology based on the utilization of light radiation. Through the lab, one will find the correlation between theory and practice and learn how to derive theories from experimental approaches within a laboratory environment.
column20: For Molecular spectroscopy (PHYS443), it's recommended to take Optics II

column19: Mathematics has been the language to express the laws of physics. Students doing physics must be trained in mathematics. Almost every branch of mathematics has been found useful to physicists. This course builds on the foundations laid in Mathematical Methods I and II. In these courses, ideas like tensors, complex analysis, integral transforms, and some special functions are discussed. It is not the purpose of this course to take the theorem-proof route which is of importance to mathematicians. Rather, it aims to cultivate a sense of thinking that has precision and rigour which are essential to physics, and a bent of mind to understand mathematical texts. Completing this will equip students to solve advanced problems in physics and other quantitative fields.

Gravity was the first of the fundamental forces of nature to be modelled mathematically. Newton’s law of gravitation was our best theory of gravity for over two centuries, and is used even today for launching space probes. Einstein, expanding on his Special Theory of Relativity, proposed the General Theory of Relativity which described gravity not as a conventional force, but as an effect of the curvature of space-time. This could explain the slight shift of planetary orbits from their Newtonian expectations, and the bending of light in the vicinity of a massive object. This theory – our most successful theory of gravity to date – is used to explain phenomena related to black holes, the recently discovered gravitational waves, and has important applications such as GPS technology. Perhaps one of the most interesting uses of General Relativity has been to model the evolution of the Universe as a whole – its expansion since the Big Bang and its possible future fate. This course covers the mathematical prelude to the study of general relativity, the formulation of Einstein’s field equations, and finally some of the applications of this theory.

Computation is processing of information. We strive for faster and energy efficient
 computation. Are there limits? Processing is carried out by physical objects obeying laws of
 physics. This informs us about possible fundamental limitations to computing. Creation of
 information costs energy. What is surprising is it cost as much energy to delete information. 
 One approach to minimize this energy cost is to do reversible computations. The conceptual
 framework to understand this is thermodynamics. Quantum theory adds further possibilities. 
 In this course, these ideas will be presented at a level accessible to undergraduates. This course
 relies more on research articles than books as the subject is still developing. An exposure to
 these ideas may help students contribute to the subject.

The Introduction of Psychology course (PSYC201) introduces students to conceptual building blocks of Psychology, including topics on perception, learning, memory, intelligence, motivation, emotion, and personality. In this way, it levels the field for students from varied educational settings in school who may have a differentiated exposure to psychology as an academic discipline, and prepares them for an undergraduate training in the field. The course seeks to facilitate students in their engagement with the lasting questions around which the discipline has evolved. PSYC201 is also designed to introduce students to some of the classic psychological studies and thereby demonstrate the principles of some of the key areas of modern psychology as a diverse and interdisciplinary science. Students will be expected to read and evaluate classic psychological research studies and critically reflect on the real-life implications of psychological insights.
column21: This is a required course for the PSYC Major, and will be offered again in T4 in the next academic year. Class size is capped at 45 with first preference given to second and third year students, and then to first year students.

column6: Introduction to Qualitative Approaches in Psychology
column19: This course is designed to introduce students to qualitative research methods. As qualitative methods gain a foothold in the field (e.g., establishment of a qualitative inquiry section within APA's Division of "Evaluation, Measurement, and Statistics," and the APA journal Qualitative Psychology; BPS recommendation for qualitative research familiarity in undergraduate courses), in this course students will be introduced to the philosophical underpinnings of qualitative approaches in psychology. Qualitative approaches subsume broad categories of thematic, narrative, language analysis, and naturalistic observation approaches. These methods are valuable for collecting rich textured data and discovering themes and categories from data, meaning from experience and the stories we tell, ways in which language is used for communicating different underlying motives, and in-depth views of human behaviour and social interaction. Students will gain an understanding of the philosophical underpinnings of both qualitative and quantitative research, knowledge of and experience with methods of collecting qualitative data; knowledge of and experience with ways of analyzing qualitative data; the ability to evaluate the quality of qualitative research (in terms of sampling, triangulation, and generalizability).

This course builds on SRM I (PSYC205) and offers more advanced methodological and statistical tools to students. The statistical techniques in the course include non-parametric tests, standardized scores, correlation, and linear regression. Students will learn to critically think about experimental procedures, sampling, randomization, manipulation, apparatus, validity issues, and ethical concerns in conducting experimental research. This course will equip students with basic skills to plan an experimental design, analyze research studies that illustrate varied experimental methods across different areas of psychology, and understand the underlying philosophy that guides empirical research. In doing so, this course provides the foundation for guided empirical research and critical analysis required in the final year of the program.

This course provides a comprehensive introduction to the theory of psychological measurement and contemporary measurement procedures utilized in psychology. Throughout the course, students will learn to interpret and use existing psychological tests and measures and develop the knowledge and proficiency to evaluate these instruments critically. This course is particularly relevant for psychology majors as it lays the foundation for a deep understanding of the reliability and validity of psychological assessments, which are essential for evidence-based practice and research in various psychology domains.

Psychological sciences probe human behavior and mental processes in a rigorous and
 systematic manner. Through this course, students will explore the implicit philosophical
 underpinnings of psychology as a science, and the kind of psychological phenomena,
 specific aims, methods emphasized, and purposes for which this knowledge is used. In
 doing so, students will reflect and review the empirical, positivistic, quantitative,
 determinable, predictive and scientific nature of psychology, addressing Giorgi’s call for
 psychology as a human science. We will then learn about a plurality of theoretical
 developments that offer new pathways for what psychology can become a discipline and
 what it means to be a human.
 Fundamentally rooted in Giorgi’s existential phenomenological approach, psychology,
 conceived of as a human science, offers an established way of understanding the life world,
 and subjective meanings as it is experienced and lived by human subjects. Drawing from
 existentialist, humanistic, and phenomenology, hermeneutics, psychoanalysis, and cultural,
 liberation and decolonial, and feminist perspectives, students will examine and reflect on the
 role of language, intersubjectivity, and interpretation in knowledge construction. Addressing
 Giorgi’s call for inventing new methods and approaches, students will tackle the problem of
 investigating the complexity of human phenomena scientifically.

This course explores foundational and contemporary perspectives on personality, self, and
 identity in psychology. It asks the fundamental question: Who are we, and what makes us who
 we are? What makes us both unique and part of a shared social world? Beginning with classical
 debates on the nature and structure of personality, students are introduced to how psychology
 has historically conceptualized the individual. The course then moves into critical examinations
 of how selfhood is shaped by social, cultural, and digital environments, as well as by
 experiences of displacement and diaspora. Drawing from diverse psychological
 traditions—including trait theory, psychoanalysis, developmental psychology, and critical/cultural
 psychology—the course investigates how identities are formed, narrated, regulated, and
 transformed. Particular emphasis is placed on Indian psychological thought, contextual
 differences, and the lived experience of navigating multiple, intersecting selves.
This course explores the neurobiological basis and psychological reality of Natural Language as a uniquely human phenomena

column6: Culture, Cognition, and Subjectivity:  Psychological Worlds Across Contexts (Formerly: PSYC345 Culture and Subjectivity)
column19:
Comprehension of cultural factors is a key to critical inquiry onto all major branches of
 psychology such as cognitive, developmental, social, and clinical. Moving across
 mainstream, critical, and non-Western approaches — with a focus on South Asian
 contexts,this course explores how human subjectivity and cognition are embedded in
 and are shaped by culture, history, and social worlds. We will examine how
 psychological processes are mediated through language, embodiment, ritual, narrative,
 and social structures like caste, gender, and coloniality.

This course is designed for advanced students of social psychology interested in pursuing questions at the boundaries of social psychological imagination. The course aims to teach the nuts and bolts of social psychological research to students who are already familiar with concepts in social psychology and are interested in honing their potential research ideas into ‘researchable’ questions. This shall be done by developing on concepts taught in social psychology to critically reading current cutting-edge research employing various methods, including experimental designs and qualitative analysis. The modules are designed to critically engage with social identity and self categorisation approaches that inform areas in psychological research.

The success of the course depends on student interest as much as instructor guidance and has been designed to integrate both equally. Students will identify their areas of interest (for example, health psychology, feminist interpretations, moral psychology, femcel mobilisation, cultural folklores, military psychology) early on in the course with the instructor’s guidance, which they will then follow with critical reading of both theoretical and empirical articles in conjunction with the modules of foundational approaches, methods, contemporary sites of behavioural analysis (including social networking sites), emotion and cognition, and social norms designed in the course. There will be a fair amount of work in this course, and it will be difficult at times – that’s the “advanced” part.

column17: Rakshi Rath, Rakesh Sengupta, Sayantan Mandal, Suryodaya Sharma
column19: This course develops on foundational concepts of social psychology and the research methods courses offered in the Psychology programme at Krea, and introduces students to the exciting world of technological mediations in psychological processes. This is primarily lab-based and will use equipments available in the psychology lab at Krea. We shall introduce students to experimental designs in immersive environments through Virtual Reality MetaQuest3 headsets, the use of EEG and Eye-tracking in studying real-world phenomena from climate change responses to social interactions to mental health interventions. The course aims to be a technologically mediated exploratory journey of social psychological research. It shall be taught by instructors of social psychology and cognitive psychology.
